question: What type of fire detection is used in the engine nacelles?

options.text: Smoke detectors sampling the nacelle ventilation air
Continuous loop detectors responding to temperature
Individual spot detectors at each nacelle fire zone
Continuous loop detectors responding to gas pressure

explanation: A continuous element covers the whole length of the zone, so a fire is detected wherever along the nacelle it starts.

question: How many detection loops are fitted to each engine?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: Two independent loops are what allow the system to distinguish a real fire from a faulty detector.

question: Under normal conditions, what is required for an engine fire warning?

options.text: Either loop alone must detect the condition
Both loops and a confirmed overheat indication
Both loops must detect the condition
One loop with the other selected inoperative

explanation: Requiring agreement is what eliminates nuisance warnings from a single damaged element.

question: What happens if one detection loop fails?

options.text: The system reverts to single loop operation on the remaining loop
The warning is downgraded to an overheat caution until maintenance
Fire detection for that engine is lost until the loop is replaced
Both loops are inhibited and a system fault light illuminates

explanation: Losing redundancy must not mean losing protection, so the surviving loop continues to give a warning on its own.

question: What is the purpose of the detector loop selector?

options.text: It transfers fire detection from the engine loops to the APU loop
It selects which of the two extinguisher bottles will discharge
It selects between the overheat and the fire sensing thresholds
It allows a single loop to be selected when the other is unserviceable

explanation: Isolating a faulty loop manually restores clean detection instead of leaving the crew with a spurious indication.

question: What do the engine detection loops sense besides fire?

options.text: An overheat condition at a lower temperature
Smoke drawn from the nacelle ventilation air
A loss of nacelle ventilation airflow
A duct leak along the bleed air ducting

explanation: The same element reports two levels, which lets a developing problem be annunciated before it becomes a fire.

question: How is an engine overheat annunciated?

options.text: By a red light without any aural alert
By an amber light and the master caution
By the fire warning bell and a red light
By a single chime and the master caution

explanation: The caution level reflects a condition that requires investigation rather than immediate shutdown.

question: How is an engine fire annunciated?

options.text: By a single chime, the master caution and a red light in the fire switch
By a bell, the master fire warning lights and a red light in the fire switch
By an amber light in the fire switch and the master caution lights
By a bell, the master caution lights and an amber light on the panel

explanation: The warning is deliberately multi sensory because it demands immediate action from whichever pilot notices it first.

question: Where are the master fire warning lights located?

options.text: On the overhead fire protection panel, one per engine
On the centre pedestal beside the engine start levers
On the glareshield, one in front of each pilot
On the forward panel below the engine displays

explanation: Placing them in the forward field of view means the warning is seen even by a pilot looking outside.

question: What is the effect of the fire warning bell cutout switch?

options.text: It resets the detection loops and clears the warning
It disarms the extinguisher squibs until the switch is pulled
It cancels both the bell and the master fire warning lights
It silences the bell while the visual warnings remain

explanation: Silencing the aural warning allows the crew to communicate, and the lights keep the condition in view until it is resolved.

question: What does pulling the engine fire switch arm?

options.text: The crossfeed valve to isolate the engine fuel
The extinguisher squibs for that engine
The engine shutdown sequence in the control unit
The automatic discharge sequence on a timer

explanation: Arming and firing are separate actions, so an agent cannot be discharged by the pull alone.

question: How is an extinguisher bottle discharged into an engine?

options.text: By pulling the fire switch fully to its second detent
By pressing a discharge button on the overhead panel
Automatically five seconds after the switch is pulled
By rotating the fire switch to the left or the right

explanation: The direction of rotation selects which of the two bottles is used, which is how a second shot is delivered.

question: How many extinguisher bottles serve the two engines?

options.text: One, shared between both of the engines
Two, and either can be discharged into either engine
Two, each one dedicated to a single engine
Four, with two dedicated to each of the engines

explanation: Sharing the bottles means both can be used on the same engine if the first discharge does not extinguish the fire.

question: Why is a second engine extinguisher bottle provided?

options.text: To allow both engines to be protected at the same time
To provide a reserve of agent for the APU compartment
To maintain a metered flow after the initial knockdown discharge
To give a second discharge if the fire warning persists after the first

explanation: The first shot may not reach or extinguish the source, and the procedure allows for a second attempt after a waiting period.

question: What does an illuminated bottle discharge light indicate?

options.text: That bottle has been discharged and is empty
The bottle pressure is above the normal range
A leak has been detected in the discharge line
That bottle is armed and ready to fire

explanation: It confirms that the agent actually left the bottle, which is different from confirming the fire is out.

question: Why is the fire switch mechanically locked?

options.text: To ensure both bottles are discharged in sequence
To prevent the switch being pulled before the bell is cancelled
To keep the squib circuits de-energised during start
To prevent an inadvertent shutdown of a serviceable engine

explanation: The consequences of pulling the wrong switch are severe, so the design requires a deliberate release before the action can be taken.

question: Which extinguishing agent is used in the fixed fire protection systems?

options.text: Halon
Carbon dioxide
Dry powder
Water

explanation: It suppresses fire effectively in enclosed spaces without damaging the equipment it is discharged onto.

question: How does Halon extinguish a fire?

options.text: It interrupts the chemical reaction of combustion
It displaces all the oxygen from the compartment
It forms a physical barrier over the burning surface
It cools the fire below its ignition temperature

explanation: Because it works chemically rather than by cooling or smothering, a relatively small quantity is effective.

question: What does the overheat and fire test verify?

options.text: That the squib circuits will fire both of the engine bottles
That the extinguisher bottles are pressurised to the correct value
That the detection loops are correctly routed along the nacelle
That the detection and warning circuits produce the correct indications

explanation: The test exercises the path from the detector to the annunciation, which is the part the crew depends on in flight.

question: What does the fault and inoperative test position reveal?

options.text: An extinguisher bottle that has lost its pressure
A failed detection loop or a break in the system
A failure of the fire warning bell or its cutout
An overheat condition developing in the nacelle

explanation: A loop that has failed silently would otherwise leave the crew believing they have dual loop protection when they do not.

question: How many detection loops protect the APU compartment?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: A single loop is accepted because the compartment is small and the APU shuts itself down when a fire is detected on the ground.

question: How many extinguisher bottles are dedicated to the APU?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

explanation: A single bottle is sufficient for a compartment of that size with no continuing fuel flow after shutdown.

question: What happens when an APU fire is detected while the airplane is on the ground?

options.text: The crew must both shut the APU down and discharge the bottle manually
The APU shuts down automatically and the bottle discharges automatically
The APU shuts down but the bottle must be discharged by the crew
The APU continues to run until the APU fire switch is pulled out

explanation: On the ground the APU may be running unattended, so the system is designed to protect the airplane without anyone in the flight deck.

question: How does the APU fire response differ in flight?

options.text: The crew must shut the APU down and discharge the bottle manually
The fire warning is inhibited above the APU bleed altitude limit
The APU shuts down but no extinguishing agent is available
The response is identical to the one on the ground

explanation: In flight the crew may still need what the APU is supplying, so the decision is left to them rather than being automatic.

question: How is the ground crew alerted to an APU fire?

options.text: By the exterior logo lights flashing
By the cabin evacuation alarm
By the passenger address system
By a horn in the nose wheel well

explanation: The alert has to reach people working outside the airplane, who cannot see the flight deck indications.

question: What is the purpose of the APU ground control panel?

options.text: It allows external power to be connected and the ground service bus to be selected
It provides a test facility for the engine and APU fire detection loops
It allows the APU to be started and run without power on the flight deck
It allows the APU to be shut down and a fire to be indicated from outside the airplane

explanation: Ground personnel who detect a problem must be able to stop the APU without going to the flight deck.

question: What protection is provided in the main wheel well?

options.text: Smoke detection only, with no warning to the crew
Neither detection nor a fixed extinguishing system
Fire detection, but no fixed extinguishing system
Both detection and a fixed extinguishing system

explanation: Detection tells the crew there is a problem, and the response uses the airflow rather than an agent.

question: What is the response to a wheel well fire warning?

options.text: Extend the landing gear to expose the wheel well to the airflow
Depressurise the cabin to starve the fire of oxygen
Reduce speed to below the gear extension limit and continue
Discharge an engine bottle into the wheel well

explanation: The airstream is the only extinguishing medium available there, and exposing the fire to it is the effective action.

question: Why is no fixed extinguishing system fitted in the wheel well?

options.text: The agent would damage the landing gear and brake components
The compartment is too large for any practical bottle size
The wheel well is classified as a ventilated rather than a fire zone
The airflow through the bay would disperse the agent before it could act

explanation: An agent needs a reasonably sealed volume to build and hold a concentration, which the wheel well cannot provide.

question: How are cargo compartment fires detected?

options.text: By continuous loop detectors
By optical flame sensors
By smoke detectors
By compartment pressure sensors

explanation: A cargo fire usually smoulders for a long time before producing heat, so smoke is what appears first.

question: Why is smoke detection more suitable than heat detection in a cargo compartment?

options.text: Smoke detectors respond without needing any electrical power
Smoke detectors are far less prone to false alarms than heat detectors
Heat detectors cannot function in an unpressurised compartment
Smouldering material produces smoke long before it produces significant heat

explanation: The aim is to detect the fire while it is still small enough for the agent to control.

question: How is agent delivered after a cargo fire discharge?

options.text: A repeated pulsed discharge at fixed timed intervals
A single large discharge with no further flow
An initial knockdown discharge followed by a metered flow
A continuous unregulated flow until the bottles are empty

explanation: The first discharge suppresses the fire and the metered flow holds the concentration while the airplane diverts.

question: Why is a metered flow used after the initial cargo discharge?

options.text: To cool the compartment structure gradually after the discharge
To maintain the agent concentration for the remainder of the flight
To avoid overpressurising the cargo compartment after discharge
To allow the smoke detectors to clear and reset themselves

explanation: A fire that is suppressed but not extinguished will reignite once the concentration falls, so it must be held until landing.

question: What happens to the airflow through a cargo compartment when the fire suppression is activated?

options.text: It is increased
It is reversed overboard
It is shut off
It is unchanged

explanation: Ventilation would both dilute the agent and supply the fire with oxygen, so the compartment is sealed as far as possible.

question: Why does the cargo fire suppression capability influence the diversion decision?

options.text: Because the bottles must be replaced before the next departure
Because the agent will maintain suppression only for a limited period
Because the smoke detectors are disabled once the agent is discharged
Because the compartment cannot be pressurised after the discharge

explanation: The suppression time sets the maximum distance to a suitable airport. Verify the capability of your fleet against your operator FCOM.

question: What determines whether a given airplane has cargo compartment fire suppression fitted?

options.text: The maximum certificated passenger capacity of that airplane
Whether the airplane is approved for extended range operations
The compartment classification and the configuration of that airplane
The number of engine extinguisher bottles that are installed

explanation: Cargo compartment protection varies between builds and operators. Verify the configuration of your fleet against your operator FCOM.

question: What does the cargo fire test confirm?

options.text: That the bottles are full and correctly pressurised
That the compartment ventilation shuts off correctly
That the detection and warning circuits are functioning
That the metered flow valve is not blocked

explanation: As with the engine system, the test exercises the annunciation path rather than the extinguishing hardware.

question: How is a lavatory fire detected?

options.text: By a continuous loop in the waste compartment
By a smoke detector in each lavatory
By a heat detector in the ceiling panel
By the cabin crew, with no automatic detection

explanation: Lavatories are unsupervised and are a recognised fire risk, so each one is monitored independently.

question: Where is a lavatory smoke alarm annunciated?

options.text: At the forward attendant station and nowhere else
In the lavatory itself and at the attendant stations
On the passenger address system and in the cabin
On the flight deck fire protection panel only

explanation: The alert must reach both the occupant and the crew who will have to respond.

question: How is the lavatory waste bin protected?

options.text: It is not protected, the bin is emptied before every flight
By a manually operated bottle mounted inside the bin
By an extinguisher that discharges automatically at a set temperature
By a smoke detector that alerts the crew to use a portable extinguisher

explanation: A waste bin fire can start unobserved, so the protection cannot depend on anyone being present to act.

question: Why does the waste bin extinguisher operate without crew action?

options.text: Because the cabin crew may not enter an occupied lavatory
Because the smoke detector cannot sense a fire inside the bin
Because a portable extinguisher would damage the bin liner
Because a fire there can develop unnoticed behind a closed door

explanation: The automatic discharge closes the gap between the fire starting and anyone discovering it.

question: What is the essential difference in crew response between an overheat and a fire indication?

options.text: An overheat requires investigation while a fire requires the engine to be shut down and the agent discharged
An overheat requires the agent to be discharged while a fire requires only the affected bleed to be isolated
A fire requires investigation while an overheat requires the engine to be shut down and secured
Both are handled the same way, and only the time available to the crew is different

explanation: The two indications describe different stages, and treating an overheat as a fire would shut down a serviceable engine unnecessarily.

question: Why is an engine fire on the ground handled differently from one in flight?

options.text: Because the detection loops are inhibited with weight on wheels
Because the fire switch is locked until the airplane is airborne
Because the extinguisher bottles cannot be discharged on the ground
Because an evacuation may be required and ground assistance is available

explanation: On the ground the passengers can be removed from the airplane, which changes the priorities of the response entirely.

question: Why is the fire warning system independent of the engine indicating system?

options.text: So that a failure of the engine displays does not remove the fire warning
Because the detection loops require AC power from a separate bus
So that the warning can be inhibited during the takeoff roll
So that the fire warning can be tested while the engines are running

explanation: A warning that depends on another system inherits that system failures, which is unacceptable for a fire indication.

question: What indication confirms that the fire has been extinguished?

options.text: The fire warning ceases
The overheat light illuminates
The bottle discharge light goes out
The loop selector returns to NORMAL

explanation: The warning is driven by the detectors, so its removal is the evidence that the condition no longer exists.

question: What should the crew consider if the fire warning persists after both bottles have been discharged?

options.text: That the APU extinguisher bottle can be selected and discharged into that engine
That the warning will clear by itself once the engine has cooled down
That the fire is not contained and the airplane must be landed as soon as possible
That the detection loop has failed and the warning can now be disregarded

explanation: With no agent remaining, time on the airframe is the only remaining variable the crew can influence.

question: Why are the engine detection loops routed along the length of the nacelle?

options.text: Because the loops must be cooled by the surrounding airflow
Because the sensing element needs a minimum installed length
Because a fire can originate anywhere in the zone
Because one element must sense both engine and pylon fires

explanation: Point detectors would leave gaps, and a fire starting in a gap would not be detected until it had spread.

question: What is the purpose of the fire protection panel test before the first flight of the day?

options.text: To verify that the cargo compartment ventilation valves close correctly
To confirm that the extinguisher bottles are pressurised correctly
To confirm that detection, warning and fault monitoring all function correctly
To reset the detection loops and the fault monitoring after the last flight

explanation: A fire system spends its entire life dormant, so the only assurance it works is a deliberate test.
